sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains that the sacrifices were offered on the outer altar and the incense on the inner altar, corresponding to the external and internal aspects of the heart, where the external heart involves enthusiasm and refinement of sparks, while the internal heart involves love and connection from the essence of the soul beyond intellect.

translations.translation: And this is also that the sacrifices were offered on the outer altar,
and the incense was on the inner altar.
For it is known that these two altars in the soul of man are the externality of the heart and the internality of the heart,
as explained in Likkutei Torah
and at length in the discourses of the Tzemach Tzedek.
Therefore the service of sacrifices is on the outer altar,
because the service that is in the aspect of enthusiasm is in the externality of the heart.
And also because in the externality of the heart the matter of refinements applies,
meaning there is still an existence that needs to be refined and elevated to holiness.
But the internality of the heart is above the matter of refinements,
and the service of the internality of the heart is the love and connection that stems from the essence of the soul, which is above reason and intellect.

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains the difference between the service of sacrifices and the service of incense regarding the things refined through them, where sacrifices involve only permitted items while incense includes impure items, and the number eleven in incense corresponds to the forces of impurity that are transformed to holiness through service in the internality of the heart.

translations.translation: And behold, the distinction between the service of sacrifices and the service of incense is also regarding the things that are refined through them.
For sacrifices are specifically from permitted things,
like all matters of Torah and mitzvos that are not fit for heavenly work except pure things and permitted in your mouth.
But the spices of the incense included impure things,
like the mor (myrrh) which is the blood of a known animal.
And also
in the incense there must specifically be eleven spices
(to the point that if one of all its spices is missing, one is liable for death,
the opposite of the matter of incense),
for the number eleven is in the side of impurity.
For it is known that in holiness the number is ten, as the saying
"ten and not nine, ten and not eleven,"
and the number eleven is in the side of impurity,
the eleven crowns of impurity.
And the explanation is,
for it is written,
"And You give life to them all,"
do not read "give life" but "bring into existence,"
that all created beings in the world, their life and also their very existence, is from Ein Sof,
and from their own perspective they have no existence at all.
And as the Baal HaHilula explains in the discourse "Mi Chamocha BaEilim Hashem, Mi Kamocha Ne'edar BaKodesh"
(which he would say once in two or three years to purify the air of the world),
that although the world is an existence and not an illusion,
nevertheless, "there is nothing besides Him,"
because the primary and true existence of every thing is the Divine power that brings it into existence.
From this it is understood,
that even the side of impurity and the husks of impurity must be said to receive vitality from Ein Sof,
for otherwise they would have no existence at all.
But the vitality that gives them life is in the aspect of an encompassing light over them from above.
[For although there is a spark of holiness also within their internality,
nevertheless, this spark is in a state of exile within them
(to the point that even the spark itself becomes like evil, as explained by the Rebbe
(the Rebbe Rashab)
of blessed memory in the discourse "Padeh BeShalom Nafshi"),
and that they live and exist is from the vitality of holiness that is in the aspect of encompassing over them from above.]
And this is that in holiness the number is ten and in the side of impurity the number is eleven.
For every thing in the world is composed of ten matters, as stated in the Pardes,
and therefore in holiness the number is ten,
because the vitality unites with the thing it gives life to and is not counted separately.
But with the husks and the side of impurity, since the vitality is in the aspect of encompassing over them from above, therefore the vitality is counted separately.
And this is that in the incense there must specifically be eleven spices,
because through the service of incense,
even the side of impurity, which is in the number eleven, is transformed into holiness.
And it can be said,
that this distinction between the service of sacrifices and the service of incense regarding the things refined through them stems from the distinction between them in the person who serves,
that the service of sacrifices is in the externality of the heart and the service of incense is in the internality of the heart.
And the explanation is,
that when the service is within measure and limitation and the person serving is still in a state of existence,
there must be caution that there be no self-interest in his service,
and certainly no self-interest from matters related to his own existence.
But when the service is above measure and limitation, then through this service,
even evil is transformed to good,
like in repentance where intentional sins become not only like unintentional sins but like merits,
[to the point that they become not only like merits
(with the "kaf" of comparison)
but actual merits],
as explained at length in Torah Or.

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains the connection of the incense service to Yom Kippur, because the repentance of Yom Kippur is the essence of repentance in the aspect of Yechidah, and since the aspect of Yechidah has no opposite, even intentional sins are transformed into merits.

translations.translation: And this is also the connection and relevance of the service of incense to Yom Kippur,
because the repentance of Yom Kippur is the essence of the matter of repentance
(supernal repentance),
and the entire service of the Ten Days of Repentance
[and certainly of Yom Kippur]
is in the aspect of Yechidah,
as is known from the teaching of the Alter Rebbe
in his explanation of the statement of our sages of blessed memory,
"Here, with the singular one," that the service of the Ten Days of Repentance is in the aspect of Yechidah,
and since corresponding to the aspect of Yechidah there is no opposite side,
"not even a trace of a trace do they have,"
therefore through the service and repentance of Yom Kippur, even intentional sins are transformed into merits.
